title: Where Does My Paycheck Go? The Full 2026 Guide

geminiStyle.dob: Say in a casual, curious young man's voice, natural podcast pace
geminiStyle.doli: Say in a warm, confident young woman's voice, clear and friendly, natural podcast pace

source: Figures from dolidob.com open data and IRS/SSA publications (2026 rules; 2027 where stated).

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Doli, I just got my first real job offer. Seventy-five thousand dollars a year!

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Congratulations! Now the question nobody asks: how much of that actually lands in your bank account?

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Seventy-five thousand divided by twenty-six paychecks. About twenty-eight hundred each time, right?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: That's your gross pay, before anything comes out. Today let's follow one paycheck from top to bottom and see where every dollar goes.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Okay. Walk me through it. Slowly.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: First stop: federal income tax. And here's the part most people get wrong. You are not taxed on all seventy-five thousand.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: I'm not?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: No. In twenty twenty-six, a single filer gets a standard deduction of sixteen thousand one hundred dollars. That part is never taxed.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: So your taxable income is fifty-eight thousand nine hundred.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: And then they take twenty-two percent of that? That's my bracket, isn't it?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Twenty-two percent is your top bracket, but only the last few dollars are taxed at that rate. The tax system works in layers.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: The first twelve thousand four hundred is taxed at ten percent. The next part, up to fifty thousand four hundred, at twelve percent. Only the rest is taxed at twenty-two.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: So what's the total?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Seven thousand six hundred seventy dollars for the year. That's about ten percent of your salary, not twenty-two.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Wait, so getting a raise can't make me take home less money?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Never. Only the dollars above the line pay the higher rate. A raise always leaves you with more.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Okay, what's next on the list?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: FICA. That's Social Security and Medicare, and they work very differently from income tax.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Social Security is a flat six point two percent of your pay. Medicare is one point four five percent. No deductions, no brackets.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: So on seventy-five thousand that's...

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Four thousand six hundred fifty for Social Security, and one thousand eighty-seven fifty for Medicare.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Does it ever stop?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Social Security does. In twenty twenty-six it stops once your wages pass one hundred eighty-four thousand five hundred. Medicare never stops, and above two hundred thousand an extra zero point nine percent is withheld.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Federal, Social Security, Medicare. Is that everything?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Not yet. Now comes the part that depends on where you live: state income tax.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Right, my offer has two locations. Texas or California.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Texas takes no income tax from wages. So on seventy-five thousand, you keep about sixty-one thousand five hundred ninety-three dollars a year.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: California takes state income tax, plus one point three percent for state disability insurance. You'd keep about fifty-seven thousand five hundred sixty-five.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: That's about four thousand dollars a year apart. For the exact same salary!

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: And Texas is not alone. Nine states take no income tax from wages: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: So I should just move to one of those?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Careful. Washington still takes paid family leave and a long-term care program, about a thousand forty dollars on seventy-five thousand. And sales tax, property tax and rent are not in your paycheck at all.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Got it. The paycheck is only one piece of the cost of living.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: One more thing. I'm getting married next year. Does that change my paycheck?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: It can. Married couples who file jointly get a bigger standard deduction, thirty-two thousand two hundred in twenty twenty-six, and wider brackets.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: If you're the only earner on seventy-five thousand, federal income tax drops from seven thousand six hundred seventy to four thousand six hundred forty.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: In Texas that means your take-home goes up to about sixty-four thousand six hundred twenty-three a year.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: That's three thousand more a year just for getting married?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: When one spouse earns and the other doesn't, yes. When you both work, the extra income fills the brackets faster, so the gap is smaller.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: How does my employer even know I'm married?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: From your Form W-4. It's the form you fill out when you start a job. It tells payroll your filing status, any second job, your dependents and extra deductions.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: If your W-4 is wrong, too much or too little comes out of every paycheck. You only find out when you file your return.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: So the W-4 is like the settings menu for my paycheck.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: That's a great way to put it. Update it when your life changes: marriage, a baby, a second job.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Got it. Life changes, update the settings.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: My friend Sam gets paid by the hour. Twenty-five dollars. How does that compare?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Full time is forty hours a week for fifty-two weeks. That's two thousand eighty hours, so twenty-five dollars an hour is fifty-two thousand a year.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: In a state with no income tax, Sam keeps about forty-three thousand nine hundred sixty-two. That's around three thousand six hundred sixty-four a month.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: And when Sam works overtime?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Under federal law, hours over forty in a week are paid at one and a half times the rate. For Sam, that's thirty-seven fifty an hour.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: But his overtime paychecks always look heavily taxed.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: That's a withholding trick, not a special tax. Payroll treats a big paycheck as if you earned that much every single week, so it withholds more. Part of it comes back at tax time.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Okay, what about bonuses? My offer mentions a five-thousand-dollar signing bonus.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Employers can withhold a flat twenty-two percent for federal tax on a bonus. That's one thousand one hundred dollars.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Then Social Security and Medicare take another three hundred eighty-two fifty. So you'd see about three thousand five hundred seventeen.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Ouch. Is the bonus taxed more than my salary?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: No. Twenty-two percent is only the amount held back up front. Your bonus is taxed like any other income when you file, so you may get some back. Only bonuses above one million dollars in a year are withheld at thirty-seven percent.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: I'll worry about the million later.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Now the part that can actually lower your taxes: your 401(k).

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: The retirement thing? I was going to skip it for now.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Here's why you shouldn't. Traditional 401(k) money comes out before federal income tax. Put in six percent, and many employers add a match.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: On a sixty-thousand-dollar salary, six percent is three thousand six hundred. A common match of fifty cents per dollar adds another eighteen hundred, free.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Free money. Okay, I'm listening. Is there a limit?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: In twenty twenty-six you can put in up to twenty-four thousand five hundred. At fifty or older, eight thousand more. And from sixty to sixty-three, a higher catch-up of eleven thousand two hundred fifty.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Roth or traditional? Everyone argues about that.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Simple rule. If you expect a lower tax rate in retirement, traditional usually wins. If you expect a higher one, Roth wins. Same rate, it's a tie.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: And next year? Does all this change?

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: The numbers move with inflation. In twenty twenty-seven the standard deduction rises to sixteen thousand six hundred, and the brackets get wider.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: On the same seventy-five thousand, federal income tax drops to about seven thousand three hundred eighty-nine. The 401(k) limit rises to twenty-five thousand five hundred.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: And Social Security will apply to wages up to one hundred ninety-two thousand three hundred.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Let me see if I've got it. Gross pay, minus the standard deduction, then tax in layers.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Plus seven point six five percent for Social Security and Medicare. Plus the state, which can be zero or several thousand.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Exactly. And then your choices: overtime, bonuses, your 401(k), your filing status. Each one changes the number.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: So the real question isn't what's my salary. It's what will I actually take home.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: That's the one. And you don't have to do the math by hand.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: At dolidob dot com there's a free paycheck calculator for every state, plus guides for everything we covered today, all built on official 2026 figures.

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: Okay, I'm checking both of my offers tonight.

lines.speaker: doli
lines.text: Good plan. These are estimates, not tax advice, so check your real pay stub too. Thanks for listening!

lines.speaker: dob
lines.text: See you next time!
